mechanism.title: The layers a read can be answered from, nearest first
steps: Client cache: the browser or app keeps responses according to Cache-Control and ETag headers. A hit costs no network at all.
CDN edge: a point of presence near the user caches static files and cacheable API responses. A hit costs one short round trip.
Reverse proxy or API gateway cache: shared responses cached in the data centre, in front of the app servers.
Application cache: an in-process map (fastest, but per server and lost on restart) or a shared cache such as Redis or Memcached (one network hop, shared by all servers).
Database buffer pool: the database keeps hot pages in RAM, so even a 'database read' is often a memory read.
On a miss at every layer, the read goes to disk or to another service, and the result is stored on the way back so the next read is a hit.

useWhen: Read-heavy data that changes rarely relative to how often it is read: product details, profiles, configuration, rendered pages.
Expensive results: aggregated counts, search results, recommendations, anything that takes many queries to build.
Static assets: images, scripts, video segments, always at the CDN.
avoidWhen: Data that must be exact on every read, such as an account balance used to approve a payment or seats left at the moment of booking; read it from the source of truth.
Write-heavy data that is rarely re-read: you pay to fill and invalidate a cache nobody hits.

rows: Hard: headers and versioned URLs only

numbers.title: Why the last few percent of hit rate matter
assumptions: Cache hit costs 1 ms, database read costs 10 ms
steps: Average latency = hit rate × 1 ms + miss rate × 10 ms.
At 90% hits: 0.9 of reads cost 1 ms and 0.1 cost 10 ms, so 0.9 + 1.0 ≈ 1.9 ms on average; database reads = 100,000 × 0.1 = 10,000 per second.
At 99% hits: 0.99 + 0.1 ≈ 1.09 ms on average; database reads = 100,000 × 0.01 = 1,000 per second.
Going from 90% to 99% cuts database load 10×, even though the hit rate only rose 9 points.
numbers.result: Database load is driven by the miss rate: 10% misses means 10,000 DB reads/s, 1% means 1,000. Quote miss rate, not just hit rate, when sizing the database.

india.title: Cricket score widgets during a big match
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: During a high-profile India match, tens of millions of people may refresh scores in news apps, streaming apps and search results. The score itself changes at most once a ball, roughly every 30–40 seconds, and is the same for everyone. So it is cached at every layer: the app keeps the last score, the CDN caches the score API response for a few seconds, and the origin reads from an in-memory cache fed by the scoring service. If 10 million clients each poll every 10 seconds, that is 1 million requests per second; with a 5-second CDN TTL, each of a few hundred edge locations refreshes about once every 5 seconds, so the origin sees on the order of a hundred requests per second or less (fewer still behind an origin shield).

pitfalls.trap: 'Add Redis' without saying what is cached or for how long.
pitfalls.say: 'I'd cache restaurant menus by restaurant ID for 5 minutes with explicit invalidation on menu edits; prices at checkout come from the database.'

pitfalls.trap: Caching data that must be strongly consistent.
pitfalls.say: 'Wallet balances are read from the primary at payment time; the cached balance is only for display.'

15.diagram:
app cache -> CDN edge -> gateway cache -> app (in-process) -> Redis -> DB buffer pool -> disk
  fastest, least shared  ------------------------------------------>  slowest, source of truth
takeaways: Cache at the layer nearest the user that can still be invalidated correctly.
Database load follows the miss rate: 99% hits means one-tenth the load of 90%.
Cache what is read often, changes rarely and is expensive to build.
Never approve money or inventory from a cache.

extraQuestions.prompt: 100,000 reads/s hit a cache. If the hit rate rises from 90% to 99%, what happens to database reads?
extraQuestions.explanation: Database reads are the misses: 10% of 100,000 = 10,000/s, then 1% of 100,000 = 1,000/s, a 10× drop.

mechanism.title: How the cache and the database stay in step under each strategy
steps: Cache-aside (lazy loading), read path: the app checks the cache; on a miss it reads the database, stores the result in the cache with a TTL, and returns it.
Cache-aside, write path: the app writes to the database, then deletes the cache key (rather than updating it) so the next read reloads fresh data.
Write-through: every write goes to the cache and the database together, and the write succeeds only when both do. Reads after writes are always warm and fresh.

Write-behind (write-back): writes go to the cache and are acknowledged immediately; the cache flushes them to the database later in batches. Very fast writes, but a cache crash before the flush loses data.
Read-through: the cache itself loads from the database on a miss (the app only talks to the cache). It behaves like cache-aside but the loading logic lives in the cache layer.
Whatever the strategy, give keys a TTL as a safety net so any missed invalidation heals itself.

useWhen: Cache-aside: the default for read-heavy services; only requested data is cached and the cache can fail without losing data.
Write-through: data that is read soon after being written and must be fresh, such as a user profile right after editing.
Write-behind: high-volume counters and metrics (likes, views) where losing a few seconds of increments is acceptable.
avoidWhen: Write-behind for money, orders or anything that must not be lost.
Write-through for data that is rarely read: every write pays for a cache entry nobody uses.

rows: Yes, if the cache dies before flushing

numbers.title: What write-behind buys and risks for a like counter
assumptions: Flush to the database every 5 seconds, batched per post
On average a hot post receives many likes per window, so each batch row covers many likes
steps: Direct writes: 20,000 database updates per second.
With write-behind, each flush writes one row per post touched; if 2,000 distinct posts are liked per 5-second window, that is 2,000 updates per flush ÷ 5 s = 400 updates per second.
Write reduction ≈ 20,000 ÷ 400 = 50×.
Risk: if the cache node dies just before a flush, up to 5 s × 20,000 = 100,000 likes are lost.
numbers.result: Write-behind turns about 20,000 writes/s into about 400, at the risk of losing up to about 100,000 likes in a crash. Fine for likes, never for payments.

india.title: Restaurant menus versus wallet balances
india.label: Illustrative design
india.body: A food delivery platform in India reads restaurant menus far more often than restaurants edit them, so menus suit cache-aside: read from Redis, on a miss load from the database, and when a restaurant edits its menu, write the database and delete the cache key. A short TTL, say 5 minutes, heals any missed delete. A digital wallet balance is the opposite case. When a user pays, the debit must happen in the database inside a transaction, and the balance used to approve the payment must come from the source of truth. A cached balance can be shown on the home screen, refreshed after each transaction, but write-behind would be unacceptable because a cache crash could lose money movements.

pitfalls.trap: Updating the cache value on write instead of deleting it.
pitfalls.say: 'I write the database, then delete the key. Concurrent writers can otherwise leave an older value in the cache.'

pitfalls.trap: Proposing write-behind for orders or payments.
pitfalls.say: 'Write-behind can lose acknowledged writes, so I'd only use it for counters; orders are written to the database first.'

16.diagram:
cache-aside read:  app -> cache? hit -> return
                          miss -> DB -> set cache(TTL) -> return
cache-aside write: app -> DB -> delete cache key
write-behind:      app -> cache (ack) ... batch flush -> DB
takeaways: Cache-aside is the safe default: read through on miss, delete the key on write, always set a TTL.
Write-through keeps reads fresh at the cost of slower writes.
Write-behind gives fast writes but can lose data; use it only where loss is tolerable.
Prefer deleting keys over updating them to avoid races.

extraQuestions.prompt: A like counter takes 20,000 likes/s and flushes from cache to the DB every 5 s. If the cache dies just before a flush, how many likes could be lost?

choices.label: None; the database already has them

extraQuestions.explanation: Five seconds of unflushed writes: 5 × 20,000 = 100,000 likes.

mechanism.title: What happens when the cache is full and a new key arrives
steps: Every cache has a memory limit. When a write would exceed it, the cache must evict something first.
LRU (least recently used) evicts the key not read for the longest time. A hash map plus a doubly linked list makes both lookup and 'move to front' O(1).
LFU (least frequently used) evicts the key with the fewest accesses, usually with counters that decay over time so yesterday's popular keys can still be evicted.
FIFO evicts the oldest inserted key regardless of use: simple, but it will evict a hot key just because it is old.
TTL expiry removes keys when their time is up, independent of memory pressure. It bounds staleness rather than size.
Production caches approximate: Redis samples a few keys (5 by default) and evicts the best candidate among them, which is close to true LRU or LFU at a fraction of the bookkeeping.

useWhen: LRU: general-purpose caches where recently used data is likely to be used again (sessions, pages, profiles).
LFU: steady popularity patterns where a one-off scan should not push out long-term favourites (product catalogue, popular videos).
TTL: anything that must not be served stale beyond a bound, layered on top of LRU or LFU.
avoidWhen: Plain LRU when big sequential scans (a nightly export) pass through the cache; they flush the hot set. LFU or scan-resistant variants handle that better.
FIFO for skewed workloads; it ignores popularity completely.

rows: One big scan evicts the hot set
Does not bound memory by itself

numbers.title: How big must the cache be for a 90% hit rate?
assumptions: 10 million products, about 2 KB of cached data each
Popularity is heavily skewed: about 20% of products receive about 90% of views (an illustrative skew; measure yours)
steps: Memory for the hot set = 2,000,000 × 2 KB ≈ 4 GB.
Caching everything would need 10,000,000 × 2 KB ≈ 20 GB.
With LRU or LFU and about 4–5 GB, the cache holds the hot set and reaches roughly 90% hits; the last 10% of hits would cost the other 16 GB.
numbers.result: About 4 GB buys roughly 90% hits under this skew; going further costs memory much faster than it adds hits. Size the cache for the hot set, then let the eviction policy keep it hot.

india.title: A video catalogue during a festival release
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Take a video streaming catalogue in India. On a normal day the popular shows stay popular for weeks, which suits LFU with decay: an occasional one-off visit to an old title should not evict a show watched by millions. On a festival weekend, though, a big new release appears and is watched heavily within hours. Pure LFU would be slow to keep it, because its count starts at zero; LRU would keep it at once. Redis offers both (allkeys-lru and allkeys-lfu), and LFU's counters decay so new hits catch up quickly. Many teams measure hit rate under both policies on a replay of real traffic before choosing.

pitfalls.trap: 'Use LRU' with no thought about the access pattern.
pitfalls.say: 'Popularity is stable and skewed, so LFU with decay; if a nightly batch scans the catalogue, I'd keep it from polluting the cache.'
'TTL bounds staleness; the eviction policy decides what goes when memory is full. I'd set both.'

17.diagram:
LRU list (most recent first):  [P9] [P2] [P7] [P1]  <- evict P1
read P7  ->                     [P7] [P9] [P2] [P1]
insert P5 (full) ->             [P5] [P7] [P9] [P2]   (P1 evicted)
takeaways: LRU evicts the least recently used key; LFU the least frequently used; FIFO the oldest inserted.
TTL bounds staleness, not memory; use it together with an eviction policy.
Size the cache for the hot set; skew means a small cache can give a high hit rate.
Real caches approximate LRU and LFU by sampling.

extraQuestions.prompt: A catalogue has 10 million items of 2 KB each, and 20% of items get 90% of views. About how much memory caches the hot set?
extraQuestions.explanation: Hot set = 20% of 10 million = 2 million items × 2 KB ≈ 4 GB.

mechanism.title: Three ways a cache fails under load, and the fix for each
steps: Stampede (thundering herd): a hot key expires, and thousands of concurrent requests all miss at once and all query the database for the same value.

Fix the stampede with request coalescing: the first miss takes a short lock (or a single-flight promise) and rebuilds the value; the others wait briefly or serve the stale value. Probabilistic early refresh rebuilds a hot key shortly before it expires.

Avalanche: many keys expire at the same moment (for example everything loaded at startup with the same 1-hour TTL), or the whole cache cluster restarts, so the database suddenly takes all the traffic.
Fix the avalanche with TTL jitter (for example 60 minutes ± 10%), staggered warm-up, a replicated cache that survives node loss, and rate limiting or circuit breakers in front of the database.
Penetration: requests for keys that do not exist (often from bots or bugs) always miss the cache and always hit the database.
Fix penetration by caching 'not found' results with a short TTL, validating IDs early, and putting a Bloom filter of existing IDs in front of the database.

useWhen: Coalescing and early refresh: any hot key with expensive rebuilds (home page feed, trending list, sale banners).
Jitter: every time you set TTLs in bulk.
Negative caching and Bloom filters: public endpoints where IDs are guessable or enumerable.
avoidWhen: Do not hold a rebuild lock without a timeout; if the rebuilder dies, everyone waits.
Do not cache 'not found' for long on data that is about to be created (a just-placed order), or users will not see their own new item.

rows: Single-flight lock, serve stale, early refresh
Many keys expire together or cache restarts
TTL jitter, warm-up, replicas, DB protection
Memory for filter; brief false 'not found' risk

numbers.title: A stampede on one hot key
assumptions: A trending-deals key is read 50,000 times per second
Rebuilding it takes 200 ms of database queries
The key expires with no protection
steps: Requests arriving during the 200 ms rebuild window = 50,000 × 0.2 = 10,000.
Without coalescing, up to 10,000 identical rebuild queries hit the database at once.
With single-flight, 1 request rebuilds and the other 9,999 wait or get the stale value.
Database queries per expiry fall from about 10,000 to 1.
numbers.result: One unprotected hot key can send about 10,000 identical queries to the database in 200 ms; coalescing makes it one.

india.title: Sale-day banners and the 'deal of the hour'
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Indian e-commerce sales often feature hourly deals that open at a fixed minute, say 'deal of the hour' at 12:00. Every shopper's app requests the same deal list at that minute, and if the cached list was given a TTL ending exactly at 12:00, the expiry and the traffic spike coincide: a textbook stampede on one key. The safer design prepares the next hour's list in advance and swaps it into the cache before 12:00, uses single-flight rebuilds in case of a miss, and adds TTL jitter to everything loaded in bulk. Bots requesting random product IDs to find unlisted deals are a penetration risk, handled with negative caching, ID validation and rate limiting.

pitfalls.trap: Treating all three problems as 'add more cache'.
pitfalls.say: 'Stampede is one hot key: coalesce. Avalanche is mass expiry: jitter and warm-up. Penetration is missing keys: negative cache and a Bloom filter.'

pitfalls.trap: Using a lock without a timeout or a stale fallback.
pitfalls.say: 'The rebuild lock has a short timeout, and waiting readers fall back to the stale value if it's not ready.'

18.diagram:
t=0  key 'deals' expires
     50K req/s --miss--> [single-flight]
                           |-> 1 rebuild -> DB
                           '-> others: serve stale / wait 50 ms
takeaways: Stampede: many misses on one hot key; fix with coalescing, stale-while-revalidate or early refresh.
Avalanche: many keys expiring together or a cache restart; fix with jitter, warm-up and replicas.
Penetration: lookups for keys that don't exist; fix with negative caching and Bloom filters.
Always protect the database behind the cache with limits.

extraQuestions.prompt: A hot key read 50,000 times/s expires and takes 200 ms to rebuild. Without coalescing, roughly how many duplicate rebuilds can hit the DB?
extraQuestions.explanation: 50,000 requests/s × 0.2 s = 10,000 requests arrive while the key is missing, each of which could trigger a rebuild.

mechanism.title: How a CDN serves a file
steps: DNS (or anycast routing) sends the user to a nearby CDN point of presence (PoP).
The edge server checks its cache for the URL. On a hit it returns the file immediately, typically within a few tens of milliseconds.
On a miss, it fetches from a regional tier or an origin shield (one designated cache in front of the origin), which in turn fetches from the origin only if it also misses.
The response is cached at the edge for as long as Cache-Control allows (max-age / s-maxage), and later requests for that URL are served locally.
For changes, give each version of a file a new URL (app.3f9c2a.js) so you can cache it for a year and still ship updates instantly; purge only for mistakes.
For private content, the app issues signed URLs or signed cookies with an expiry; the edge checks the signature, so it can serve paid video without calling your servers.

useWhen: Static assets: images, scripts, stylesheets, fonts, app bundles.
Video: segments for HLS and DASH streaming, which are ideal cache objects.
Cacheable API responses that are the same for many users for a few seconds (scores, prices on listing pages, configuration).
avoidWhen: Personalised or authenticated responses without careful cache keys; a shared cache can leak one user's data to another.
Data that must be exact per request (checkout totals, seat availability at booking).

rows: Versioned URLs (content hash in the name)
None; old files simply age out
Seconds to minutes across all PoPs
Easy to forget a URL; a purge storm hits the origin

numbers.title: Egress for a live stream with and without a CDN
assumptions: Average bitrate 2 Mbit/s (a mix of mobile qualities)
Video split into 6-second segments; each edge fetches each segment from the shield once
steps: Total delivery bandwidth = 10,000,000 × 2 Mbit/s = 20,000,000 Mbit/s = 20 Tbit/s, all served by CDN edges.
Without a CDN, the origin itself would have to push about 20 Tbit/s.
With a CDN, each edge fetches each segment about once per rendition, so the origin or shield serves roughly 500 edges × a handful of renditions per segment.
Origin egress ≈ 500 × 2 Mbit/s × 5 renditions = 5,000 Mbit/s = 5 Gbit/s, about 4,000× less than 20 Tbit/s.
numbers.result: The CDN carries about 20 Tbit/s at the edges while the origin sends a few Gbit/s. Live streaming at this scale is only possible because each edge fetches each segment once.

india.title: Live cricket at record concurrency
india.label: Publicly reported concurrency; bandwidth is an illustrative estimate
india.body: Indian streaming services have publicly reported record live audiences for cricket: Disney+ Hotstar reported about 25.3 million concurrent viewers during the 2019 World Cup semi-final between India and New Zealand, and later reported higher peaks for subsequent tournaments. At an illustrative average of 2 Mbit/s per viewer, 25 million viewers need about 50 Tbit/s of delivery capacity, far beyond any single origin. That load is spread across CDN PoPs, including caches placed inside Indian internet providers' networks, while the origin produces each 6-second segment once per quality level. Capacity is planned and pre-provisioned with CDN partners well before a big match, because autoscaling cannot add terabits in minutes.

pitfalls.trap: Relying on purges to ship new JavaScript.
pitfalls.say: 'Assets get content-hashed file names and a one-year max-age; index.html is short-lived and points at the new hashes.'

pitfalls.trap: Serving paid video from public URLs.
pitfalls.say: 'The app issues short-lived signed URLs or cookies; the edge verifies the signature without calling our servers.'

19.diagram:
viewers -> [edge PoP Mumbai] --miss--> [origin shield] --miss--> [origin / packager]
viewers -> [edge PoP Delhi ] --hit--> (served locally)
takeaways: A CDN serves from caches near users; the origin is hit only on misses.
Version asset URLs and cache them for a long time; purge only by exception.
Use signed URLs or cookies for private content.
For big live events, the edge carries terabits while the origin sends each segment once per rendition.

extraQuestions.prompt: 10 million viewers watch a live stream at an average of 2 Mbit/s. What total delivery bandwidth must the CDN edges provide?

mechanism.title: What happens inside Redis when you run a command
steps: Redis keeps all data in RAM and executes commands one at a time on a single main thread, so each command is atomic without locks. Network I/O can use extra threads in newer versions, but command execution stays single-threaded.

Because commands are tiny in-memory operations, a single node typically serves on the order of 100,000+ simple operations per second with sub-millisecond latency, until one slow command (KEYS *, a huge SORT) blocks everyone behind it.

Data structures do the work on the server: strings and counters (INCR), hashes (objects), lists (queues), sets, sorted sets (leaderboards, rate-limit windows), streams (append-only logs), plus HyperLogLog and bitmaps.
Persistence is optional: RDB snapshots write the whole dataset periodically; the AOF appends every write and can fsync every second, losing at most about a second of writes on a crash.
Replication is asynchronous: a replica follows the primary's stream of writes. If the primary fails, a replica is promoted, and writes not yet replicated can be lost.

Redis Cluster splits the key space into 16,384 hash slots spread across primaries. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16,384; hash tags like {user:42} keep related keys in one slot so multi-key commands still work.

useWhen: Caches, sessions, rate limiting counters, leaderboards (sorted sets), short-lived locks, lightweight queues and pub/sub.
Anywhere you need atomic operations on small shared state at high throughput: INCR, ZADD, SET with NX and expiry.
avoidWhen: As the only copy of data you cannot lose, given asynchronous replication and memory-bound capacity.
Datasets far larger than RAM, or workloads needing complex queries and joins.

numbers.title: A live leaderboard for a quiz show
assumptions: 5 million players in one sorted set
About 64 bytes per entry including member ID and overhead (an estimate; check with MEMORY USAGE)
200,000 score updates per second at peak
steps: Memory = 5,000,000 × 64 bytes = 320,000,000 bytes ≈ 320 MB, which fits easily on one node.
ZADD and ZRANK are O(log N); log2 of 5 million is about 22, so each operation is a few dozen steps.
200,000 updates per second is above what one node handles comfortably, so split players into shards (for example 4 sorted sets by player ID), giving 50,000 updates per second per shard.
Global top 10 = take the top 10 from each of the 4 shards (40 entries) and merge them.
numbers.result: About 320 MB of memory and O(log N) updates: sorted sets make a 5-million-player leaderboard cheap. Shard by player and merge the per-shard top 10s for the global top 10.

india.title: Fantasy and quiz contests during IPL
india.label: Illustrative estimate
india.body: Fantasy sports and live quiz apps in India see huge, synchronised spikes: when a wicket falls in an IPL match, millions of contest scores change at the same moment and players immediately check their rank. A sorted set per contest gives O(log N) score updates and rank lookups, and the whole leaderboard for a large contest fits in a few hundred megabytes. The heavy part is the write burst, so updates are batched per ball, contests are spread across many Redis primaries by contest ID, and very large contests are sharded internally. Final results and payouts are computed from the durable database, not from Redis, because Redis replication is asynchronous.

pitfalls.trap: Running KEYS * or a huge range query in production.
pitfalls.say: 'I'd use SCAN with a cursor and keep operations bounded; one slow command blocks the single command thread.'

pitfalls.trap: Using Redis as the system of record for money or orders.
pitfalls.say: 'Redis replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose recent writes; the database is the source of truth.'

20.diagram:
client -> CRC16(key) mod 16384 = slot 9842
slots 0-5460     -> primary A (+replica)
slots 5461-10922 -> primary B (+replica)   <- slot 9842
slots 10923-16383-> primary C (+replica)
takeaways: Redis executes commands on one thread in RAM: fast and atomic, but slow commands block everyone.
Pick the data structure for the job: sorted sets for rankings, hashes for objects, streams for logs.
Replication is asynchronous; persistence is optional. Don't make Redis your only copy of critical data.
Redis Cluster shards keys over 16,384 slots; use hash tags to co-locate related keys.

extraQuestions.prompt: How does Redis Cluster decide which node owns a key?

choices.label: CRC16 of the key mod 16,384 gives a slot, and each primary owns a range of slots
Keys are assigned round robin as they are written
The client picks any node; nodes copy all keys to each other
The key's first letter picks the node

extraQuestions.explanation: Redis Cluster has 16,384 hash slots. A key's slot is CRC16(key) mod 16,384, and slots are distributed across primaries.
